item.title: Pentagon UAP files part 8: Radar track analysis and more - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• The U.S. Pentagon released the 8th batch of its UAP files on November 20, 2026.
  • This Pentagon UAP files release contains 43 new files altogether. Among these, 40 are documents and three are videos.
  • The release is part of a continuing rollout of formerly classified files, every few weeks. So far, there’s still been no “smoking gun” to show that alien craft are visiting Earth. But the files are interesting!

The 2027 lunar calendar from EarthSky is now available! See the moon’s phase for every day of the year. Makes a great gift! Order yours today.

8th batch of Pentagon UAP files

The U.S. Pentagon released its 1st batch of declassified UAP/UFO materials on May 8, 2026. On Friday, November 20, it released batch 8. There are 43 new files in batch 8, 40 PDF documents (some with images) and three videos. There are no audio or separate image files this time around, however.

Some of the documents are older again, but others are from this year.

And as has been the pattern for these releases, they are a mixed bag of old and previously known material and newer material. Do the releases prove aliens exist, or that alien craft are visiting Earth? No. Not so far, across any of the eight releases.

As usual, Sean Parnell, Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Public Affairs and Chief Pentagon Spokesman, said in a statement:

Today, the Department of War is publishing the 8th release of declassified and historical Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) files as part of the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE). The collection continues to be housed on WAR.GOV/UFO, and the Department will release additional files on a rolling basis.

The Department of War and our agency partners are actively working on the next release of UAP files. The 8th release of UAP files is available now on WAR.GOV/UFO.

For context, the government released a 2nd batch on May 22, a 3rd batch on June 12, the 4th batch on July 10, the 5th batch on August 7, the 6th batch on September 18 and the 7th batch of the Pentagon UAP files on October 23, all in 2026. 

1st analysis of radar tracks

One of the more interesting cases in this batch is a series of unusual radar tracks in the western U.S. from 2023. A civil air-surveillance radar system recorded eight detections over 84 seconds at an estimated altitude of 55.000-70.000 feet (16,760-21,300 meter).

The distance between the tracks was 38.5 miles (62 km). The analysis suggested that if it was just one object causing the tracks, then it had a groundspeed of 1,650 mph (2,700 kph), or approximately Mach 2.5 at the reported altitude.

Additionally, there was also an apparent 39-degree counterclockwise change in bearing after approximately 48 seconds.

The 12-second radar sweep interval, however, is not sufficient to independently establish that all eight reported detections originated from the same object or represent a continuous track.

3 videos from the Middle East in Pentagon UAP files

There are only three videos in this release, all from the Middle East.

The 1st video is from the United States Central Command, which submitted a report of an unidentified anomalous phenomenon (UAP) to the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO). The 20-second-long footage is from a U.S. military platform in 2020.

The object (or area of contrast as the DoD calls it), a tiny dot in the video, passes by a warship.

The 2nd video is also from the United States Central Command and submitted to AARO. It consists of 54 seconds of video footage from an electro-optical and infrared system aboard a U.S. military platform in 2026.

It shows multiple objects, dots again, moving over the ocean.

The 3rd video, again from the United States Central Command and submitted to AARO, is 13 seconds long. An electro-optical and infrared system aboard a U.S. Military platform obtained the footage in 2023.

It is similar to the 1st two videos, showing a small dot-like object. In this one, however, the object makes sudden, sharp changes in direction.

Assessment of national security issues relating to ‘Flying Saucers,’ 1952

This document from 1952 is interesting. It is a memorandum from S. Q. Reber, Assistant Director for Intelligence Coordination, to the Deputy Director (Intelligence). It provides an assessment of national security issues relating to “flying saucers.”

And there is an interesting reference to psychological warfare in the conclusion. It says:

It is far too early in view of the present state of our knowledge regarding Flying Saucers for psychological warfare planners to start planning how the United States might use U.S. Flying Saucers against the enemy.

Lockheed UAP report, 1953

There is also the full UAP report from leading Lockheed aerospace engineer Kelly Johnson (associated with the spy planes U-2 and SR-71) and Lockheed’s top test pilots/engineers. The incident occurred near Agoura and Point Mugu, California, on December 16, 1953. The report description states:

This report is significant, due to Johnson’s reputation as one of the foremost aerospace engineers in American history, and his virtually unmatched familiarity with high-performance aircraft.

Johnson reported observing a dark, elliptical object from his ranch west of Agoura at approximately 5 p.m. He initially considered whether it might be a cloud or smoke trail; he reported that it appeared stationary for several minutes before moving westward and disappearing.

At about the same time, personnel aboard a Lockheed test flight reported seeing an object in the vicinity of Point Mugu while flying off the southern California coast. Their accounts described a similar stationary, dark, wing-like or elongated object that also moved westward and disappeared from view.

Johnson himself said:

I should state that for at least five years I have definitely believed in the possibility that flying saucers exist; this in spite of a good deal of kidding from my technical associates. Having seen this particular object on December 16th, I am now more firmly convinced than ever that such devices exist, and I have some highly technical converts in this belief as of that date.

BAASS 10-month report

The July 2009 10-month report from BAASS (Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Studies) is also included in this batch. It’s long, at 538 pages. The report was part of a Defense Intelligence Agency program, AAWSAP (Advanced Aerospace Weapon Systems Applications Program), funded by Congress. Senator Harry Reid pushed for the program, to study potential future aerospace threats and UAP.

The report highlighted the need for:

… a highly secure underground vault to store hardware and biological samples from the corporate world and/or from private individuals and groups located elsewhere, including Brazil.

The report added:

It was recognized by the BAASS administrator that there was no highly secure facility at BAASS to store exotic material or tissue that the organization could obtain. Accordingly, the BAASS administrator designed an underground facility to be located in North Las Vegas at the Bigelow Aerospace facility.

It would be buried under 15 to 20 feet of dirt and feature a 5,000-square-foot (465-square-meter) vault with 3-foot-thick (1-meter-thick) walls and a thick steel door. It would be camouflaged on the ground. The facility was reportedly never built, however.

Bottom line: The U.S. government released the 8th batch of Pentagon UAP files on November 20, 2026. They include three videos from the Middle East and numerous documents.

item.title: BepiColombo goes into orbit around Mercury today! - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
A new mission to Mercury, BepiColombo, will send its 2 spacecraft into orbit around Mercury on November 21, 2026. BepiColombo launched in 2018. Why has it taken 8 years to get to Mercury? EarthSky’s Will Triggs explains.

Science news, night sky events and beautiful photos, all in one place. Click here to subscribe to our free daily newsletter.

BepiColombo mission to go into orbit around Mercury today

The two science orbiters in the European Space Agency’s Bepicolombo mission will go into orbit around Mercury at at 12:24 CST (18:24 UTC) today (November 21, 2026). They’ll provide our first closeup look at the sun’s innermost planet since NASA’s MESSENGER spacecraft — previously the first and only craft ever to orbit Mercury — ended its mission in 2015.

Bepicolombo launched to space way back on October 20, 2018, from Kourou, French Guiana. The spacecraft spent eight years maneuvering into position so that it can orbit Mercury, the closest planet to the sun. Orbiting Mercury is a true engineering challenge, because the spacecraft picks up speed as it nears the massive sun. So Bepicolombo had to slow down to enter Mercury’s orbit and not fly straight past the planet.

During its eight-year journey toward our sun’s innermost planet, BepiColombo made flybys — designed to help it hit the brakes — of Earth, Venus and Mercury itself. On September 3, 2026, ESA said that Bepicolombo’s Mercury Transfer Module (the spacecraft’s propulsion unit) had successfully separated from the two science orbiters. Those orbiters are called the Mercury Planetary Orbiter and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter. That was a crucial step in enabling them to enter orbit around a planet so near our local star. The two orbiters will separate from each other on December 9-10, 2026. Science operations will begin in April 2027.

For mission updates, follow ESA Operations on Bluesky.

BepiColombo’s flybys

BepiColombo has made one Earth flyby, two Venus flybys, and six Mercury flybys since its launch in 2018. Click the links below to learn more about the flybys.

April 10, 2020: 1st Earth flyby
October 15, 2020: 1st Venus flyby
August 10, 2021: 2nd Venus flyby
October 1, 2021: 1st Mercury flyby
June 23, 2022: 2nd Mercury flyby
June 20, 2023: 3rd Mercury flyby
September 4, 2024: 4th Mercury flyby
December 1, 2024: 5th Mercury flyby
January 8, 2025: 6th Mercury flyby

What scientists hope to learn at Mercury

Mercury is currently the least-understood planet in the inner solar system. In fact, before BepiColombo, the only spacecraft to have visited Mercury were NASA’s Mariner 10 and MESSENGER missions.

Now, scientists hope to solve five mysteries with BepiColombo:

  1. Where did Mercury come from?
  2. Is there really water on Mercury?
  3. Is Mercury dead or alive?
  4. Why is Mercury so dark?
  5. Why does Mercury have a magnetic field?

To answer these questions, BepiColombo will spend at least one year orbiting Mercury. The mission will use its high-resolution instruments to learn about the mineralogical and elemental composition of Mercury’s surface. Plus, it will scan polar regions for ice. BepiColombo will look for anything that looks like it has changed on Mercury since MESSENGER visited 10 years earlier. And the two orbiters will travel through different areas of the planet’s magnetosphere to measure how it changes and interacts with the sun.

Bottom line: The BepiColombo mission has been maneuvering its way into orbit around Mercury for eight years. On November 21, the two spacecraft will finally enter orbit around Mercury.

Via ESA

item.title: Artemis astronauts on the moon will see Earth upside down - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Artemis astronauts on the moon will see Earth upside down

In 2028, the astronauts of Artemis 4 are scheduled to end a more than 50-year absence of humans on the moon’s surface. How will their experience compare with that of the Apollo astronauts? For one thing, Artemis astronauts will see Earth comparatively “upside down.”.Plus, they’ll walk in shadows that stretch for miles.

Apollo astronauts visited six different sites that were on the moon’s northern hemisphere or close to the equator. In contrast, Artemis astronauts will be near the south pole, taking advantage of the low angle of the sun, where craters can be in permanent shade and possibly harbor stores of water ice.

Of course, there’s no single correct orientation for Earth, or any celestial body for that matter. But Earth will look upside down to Artemis astronauts compared to the typical perspective of a globe with north at top. We experience the same thing viewing the moon from Earth. When those of us in the Northern Hemisphere look at the moon, we see more lunar maria (dark plains) at the top, while Southern Hemisphere observers see those features at the bottom of the moon.

Plus, the view of Earth “upside down” will be more pronounced than viewing a full moon on Earth. Since Earth is of course larger than our moon, our planet will appear to loom more than 3 1/2 times bigger in the moon’s sky than a full moon looks to earthlings.

Love the moon? You’ll love EarthSky’s lunar calendar. See the phase of the moon for every day of 2027. Order yours now!

The moon’s southern hemisphere

In the 60s and 70s, Apollo astronauts aimed for the big volcanic plains — or maria — for their landings and explorations. Artemis astronauts will be exploring a different landscape. If we’re ever to establish a moon base, we’ll need water, and the best place to find that is in deep shadows in the southern hemisphere. The southern hemisphere is more rugged than the north, with craters, towering ridges and permanently shadowed regions.

At the Apollo landing sites, the sun climbed relatively high in the sky. At the lunar south pole, it will barely rise. At some of the targeted landing locations, the sun will never climb more than about 7 degrees above the horizon.

That low angle will cast extraordinarily long shadows across the desolate lunar landscape. A mountain or crater rim many miles away could cast a shadow across the astronauts’ path. This could affect astronaut’s ability to navigate, because they might have trouble judging depths and spotting hazards.

The differences in light and shadow can also create great contrasts in temperature. Areas that sit in permanent shadows can have temperatures as low as -334 F (-203 C). Meanwhile, areas in nearby sunshine can be much warmer. The moon’s near-complete lack of atmosphere contributes to this stark temperature difference.

The strange view from the lunar surface

Because the moon is only about 1/4 the size of Earth, the horizon appears much closer. So, on the lunar surface, the horizon appears only about 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) away when on flat terrain.

Astronauts on the moon don’t get to see colorful sunsets. Again, because there’s no real atmosphere, the sunlight doesn’t scatter air particles. So there isn’t a blue sky, either. The sky will always be black. This also means astronauts can see stars in the daytime, but only if they stand in a shadow to lessen the glare of the sun and the reflective lunar surface. Although stars don’t appear in photos taken from the moon’s surface (why?), the Apollo astronauts said that when they stood in the shadow of the lunar lander, they were able to see stars.

The lack of an atmosphere also means the moon is incredibly quiet. You can’t hear your own footsteps … or footsteps of anyone sneaking up on you. The surface also doesn’t experience weathering like we’re used to. So if an astronaut wanders too far and gets lost, they can just follow their footprints back to where they started.

Bottom line: Artemis astronauts will explore the moon’s south polar region, so Earth will appear “upside down” to them. Here are more strange things the astronauts will experience on the moon.

item.title: Mystery space object moves in strange ways - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• 1998 KY26 is an unusual object that orbits the sun between Earth and Mars. What is it?
  • The mystery space object sometimes accelerates in ways that gravity alone doesn’t explain.
  • Photons of light from the sun might explain the strange movements of 1998 KY26, a new study suggests.

EarthSky’s famous lunar calendar is now available. Our beautiful blue and silver poster shows every day’s moon phase for 2027. Order yours today!

Mystery space object puzzles astronomers

An unusual object is orbiting the sun between Earth and Mars. It’s called 1998 KY26, and it’s not particularly big; it’s only about 36 feet (11 meters) across. But it accelerates around the sun in ways that gravity can’t account for. What is this object, and why’s it moving like that?

This object has been theorized to be a comet, an asteroid, or even an old space probe. But scientists now think it’s most likely an asteroid. And as for its strange movements, a new study suggests photons from the sun might be the key.

Korbin Hansen and Masatoshi Hirabayashi at the Georgia Institute of Technology published their new peer-reviewed paper in Icarus on October 28, 2026.

Alexander Nazaryan wrote about the latest findings in The New York Times on November 16, 2026.

Unusual accelerations

It’s the movements of 1998 KY26 that made it stand out to astronomers. It exhibits peculiar accelerations that cause it to deviate from its normal orbit around the sun. Johannes Kepler’s laws of planetary motion say that it should maintain a nice, neat orbit.

So why is it accelerating?

Various hypotheses for mystery space object

Scientists have proposed various hypotheses for the mystery space object. Is it a comet? 1998 KY26 doesn’t have a tail, which we’d expect a comet to have. But dark comets don’t have tails. Could it be a dark comet?

The researchers think not. In the new study, they show that the object is too warm to be a comet. Its temperature is -53 degrees Fahrenheit (-47 degrees Celsius). That’s cold, but it’s too warm for ice to exist on the object in space. Darryl Z. Seligman at Michigan State University said in The New York Times:

If something has ice, then it’s a comet. But no ice means no comet. The surface of KY26 is too warm.

Near-Earth Objects (NEOs) like 1998 KY26 are difficult to study, even though they are relatively close. That’s because they are typically very small. As Seligman noted:

There’s not tons of data on very Near-Earth Objects. They’re super small and faint.

Is 1998 KY26 powered by the sun?

In 2025, another paper showed that the object was actually only 1/3 the size that scientists thought it was. That was significant. It meant that other forces could be at work besides gravity to explain the acceleration.

Davide Farnocchia, a navigation engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California, came up with an intriguing idea. Is the sun causing the unusual movements of 1998 KY26? If so, then photons — the smallest possible particles of electromagnetic energy — might be pushing the object. This phenomenon is called radiation pressure.

David Jewitt is the director of the Institute for Planets and Exoplanets at the University of California, Los Angeles. He explained:

Light photons carry momentum; it’s very small per photon, but there’s a hell of a lot of photons. That pressure is enough to push bodies around if they’re not too big.

There’s another force too, called the Yarkovsky effect. That’s when an object radiates heat after absorbing sunlight. That could be at play on the object as well. And the combination of the two forces might explain the accelerations of 1998 KY26.

Phobos 1?

There’s another very different possibility that has been floated as well. Could the object be the old Soviet Phobos-1 probe? The Soviet Union launched it back in 1998. Its mission was to visit Mars. But it was lost and never heard from again.

Avi Loeb at Harvard University has offered this as a possible explanation. You remember Avi? He famously suggested that the interstellar comet ‘Oumuamua was more likely to be an alien spaceship.

But he doesn’t think 1998 KY26 is a spaceship. Instead, he thinks it could be the Phobos 1 probe. He first proposed this last May in a paper that he co-authored.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, however, said there is no evidence that it is:

… anything but an asteroid.

 Bryce T. Bolin, a scientist at Eureka Scientific Inc., added:

There’s all sorts of space junk out there, but this object is way too heavy, way too dense.

Japan’s Haybusa2 spacecraft was supposed to visit 1998 KY26 in 2031. But just this month, the Japanese space agency called off that plan due to reported engine problems.

Bottom line: 1998 KY26 is a mystery space object that accelerates in ways that gravity alone can’t explain. A new study suggests light photons from the sun as the cause.

Source: Thermally unfavorable conditions of volatile existence in near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26, the Hayabusa extended mission’s target

Via The New York Times

item.title: T. rex babies were the size of kittens, new study says. Aw! - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
T. rex babies were the size of kittens!

We might think of T. rex dinosaurs as giant apex predators, but they didn’t start out life that way. When T. rex babies hatched from eggs, they were the size of kittens, researchers from the University of Saskatchewan said on November 17, 2026.

Adult T. rexes could span up to 40 feet (12 meters) from nose to tail, and weighed up to 15,000 pounds (7,000 kg). And momma T. rexes would lay from 30 to 100 eggs at a time, says the new study. The emerging pint-sized hatchlings were largely left to fend for themselves, so most T. rex babies likely ended up as prey instead of predators.

The researchers published their peer-reviewed study in the journal Biology on July 7, 2026.

EarthSky’s famous lunar calendar is now available. Our beautiful blue and silver poster shows every day’s moon phase for 2027. Get yours now!

Investigating the T. rex fossils

Nick Longrich of the University of Bath discovered the tiny fossils in museum collections. He and his colleagues called on the help of the Canadian Light Source synchrotron at the University of Saskatchewan for further analysis. A synchrotron produces different kinds of light — such as X-rays — to study specimens at the molecular level.

Thus, the synchrotron allowed researchers a closer look inside the fossilized bones. They were able to see blood vessels, growth patterns and changes in bone density in the bones of the T. rex babies. This data led them to a size estimate of the babies. And it also showed that these were indeed fossils from baby T. rexes and not embryos.

What fossils say about the life of a baby T. rex

When animals have a large number of babies instead of few, they are using a strategy known as r-selection. Animals with lots of babies don’t do a lot of parenting. The babies are largely left to fend for themselves, and hopefully with the large numbers it means at least some will survive. (For example, consider the ocean sunfish, which can give birth to 300 million babies at a time!)

Longrich said:

There just would’ve been tons of these little dinosaurs running around. And then you never find them because they all get eaten.

Longrich thinks T. rexes probably did a little parenting, but not much. More than, say, crocodiles and turtles, but less than birds. Longrich said:

They were starting to become better parents, but they weren’t quite there yet. It wasn’t this helicopter parent, like, just, you know, hovering over its offspring, protecting them, feeding them. It’s just kind of a … more of a free-range parent. You know, it’s, ‘Come on, kids. Don’t get eaten. We’re going this direction.’

Watch a short video about the T. rex fossils

Bottom line: T. rex babies were the size of kittens. A new study that analyzed the fossils of juvenile T. rex bones suggests parents were largely hands off.

Source: Hatchlings of Tyrannosaurus rex and the Evolution of Dinosaur Reproductive Strategies

Via University of Saskatchewan

item.title: What do baby stars sound like? Listen to them here! - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
The 2027 lunar calendar from EarthSky is now available! See the moon’s phase for every day of the year. Get yours now!

What do baby stars sound like?

NASA creates sonifications of astronomical data by translating digital data from telescopes into musical notes and sounds. Each layer of sound in these videos represents particular wavelengths of light, So now we can both see and hear these distant space objects. NASA released this signification batch on November 17, 2026, and the focus is on areas where stars are being born.

The first three sonifications are from stellar factories in our Milky Way Galaxy: the star clouds Rho Ophiuchi, the Orion Nebula and the Carina Nebula. Lastly we take a look at M82, which astronomers call a starburst galaxy because its rate of star formation vastly outstrips that of our own galaxy.

Rho Ophiuchi star cloud

The sounds of the star cloud Rho Ophiuchi are at top. This star cloud is known for its striking kaleidoscope of color. The Chandra X-ray telescope allows astronomers to cut through the dust to the infant stars within. They are violent young things flaring with X-rays. The scientists paired this data with infrared data from Webb. NASA said:

When scientists make this data audible, Chandra’s X-rays become high-pitched glassy tones, along with other sustained sounds to mark the appearance of extended bright sources. The clouds in Webb’s infrared data are mapped as differently pitched sounds, and stars are played as metallic plucks. There is a gap in the middle of the piece however, due to dark dust clouds that emit very little light.

Baby stars in the Orion Nebula nursery

The Orion Nebula is a stellar nursery that you can see with your eyes alone! Look toward the Orion constellation with its familiar Belt, which consists of three stars in a row. Just below the Belt dangles Orion’s Sword. And on that Sword you’ll notice a misty patch around a star. That’s the Orion Nebula.

This is one of the closest star-forming regions to Earth, at a distance of 1,300 light-years. Chandra can see more than 1,000 newborn stars here. NASA said:

In the sonified version of the Chandra data, these stars are twinkling sounds. Scientists map the diffuse X-ray emission to pure high tones. An infrared image from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the raw material of dust and gas used to build these new stars, and its data is heard as lower musical tones, distorted string instruments and a digital harp.

The notes of the Carina Nebula

The Carina Nebula is a massive cloud of gas and dust that spans three times the size as a full moon in our sky. This stellar factory lies in Southern Hemisphere skies in the constellation Carina the Keel. Inside the Carina Nebula are a couple famous objects, including the exploding star Eta Carinae and the Homunculus Nebula.

The portion of the Carina Nebula that we see in the video below is from the Webb space telescope. Astronomers gave it the nickname of the Cosmic Cliffs. NASA said:

Chandra also looks at this region, seeing through the dust and gas, and detects individual baby stars, which are turned into short string sounds in the sonification. A diffuse X-ray glow throughout the region has longer strings notes assigned to it. The nebula in the Webb data is mapped to a sustained sound, punctuated by other instruments to denote features like stars and ridges.

Listening to another galaxy, M82

The galaxy M82 is a starburst galaxy, because its rate of star formation is some 100 times more prodigious than our own galaxy. M82 lies 12 million light-years away in the direction of the constellation Ursa Major. Why is it so active compared to our galaxy? Scientists think it might have experienced a collision with another galaxy sometime in the past. The sonfication below combines data from Chandra, Webb, Hubble and Spitzer. The result? A dripping, clanking, windy soundscape! NASA said:

The sonification of the three types of light begins with a radar-like scan that is louder where sources are brighter. The X-ray data is mapped to the highest range of frequencies heard. Infrared data is heard as a low drone plus plucked sounds, while the optical data turns into a range of musical pitches and textures.

Bottom line: NASA shared four new sonifications — or soundscapes created from data — of stellar factories in our universe. Listen to what these baby stars sound like!

Gazing toward our galaxy’s south window into intergalactic space

When you gaze toward the bright star Fomalhaut, in the constellation Piscis Austrinus the Southern Fish, you’re looking toward what you might call our galaxy’s south window. That is, you’re looking away from the flat plane of our Milky Way, where most of our galaxy’s stars reside.

But you’re not looking in complete opposite direction of our galaxy’s core. Instead, you ‘re looking up toward one of the galaxy’s poles. When you look at Fomalhaut, you are looking some 90 degrees from the plane of our galaxy’s equator.

Most of the galaxy’s stars reside in its flat plane. So — to the eye — the region of the sky around Fomalhaut looks relatively empty. That’s why it’s known as the Loneliest Star. But beyond Fomalhaut, and beyond other Milky Way stars in this direction of space — beyond your ability to see with the eye alone — you’re gazing into the vast space between galaxies.

Voilà! You’re looking out the galaxy’s south window.

The Milky Way’s south galactic pole

Our Milky Way Galaxy is round and flat, like a pancake. So when you look toward Fomalhaut, you’re looking away from the pancake, and out the south window of the galaxy. In other words, we’re looking above the star-packed disk of the galaxy, into intergalactic space and the realm of galaxies.

Want the exact location of the south galactic pole? It lies east of Fomalhaut, in the faint constellation Sculptor. See the chart below.

Finding Fomalhaut

Fomalhaut is a very noticeable star because it’s in a region of the heavens where there are few stars bright enough to be seen with the eye. That’s why Fomalhaut is often called the Loneliest Star.

If you’re not sure which star is Fomalhaut, try using the Great Square of Pegasus as a guide. The Great Square of Pegasus appears in the south to overhead by around 7 to 8 p.m. local time in late November and early December. You’ll notice this large asterism — or pattern of stars — really does look like a large square, with four medium-bright stars marking the corners. Then draw a line from the two westernmost stars downward to Fomalhaut. See the chart below.

What about from the Southern Hemisphere? Look for the Great Square to the north around 9 to 10 p.m. local time in late November and early December. Then draw a line from the two westernmost stars upward to Fomalhaut.

Bottom line: Use the Great Square of Pegasus to locate the star Fomalhaut. Once you’ve found Fomalhaut, you’re on your way to looking out our galaxy’s south window into intergalactic space.

item.title: Will Voyager 1 ever again be closer than 1 light-day? - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Will Voyager 1 ever again be closer than 1 light-day?


The two Voyager spacecraft launched from Earth in 1977. They visited the outer planets in the 1980s and have been traveling outward ever since. Only 5 spacecraft launched from Earth have ever gone toward interstellar space (the two Voyagers, two Pioneers and New Horizons). Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in 2012, NASA said. Voyager 2 entered interstellar space in 2018. Neither craft will ever return to Earth.

And Voyager 1 achieved an incredible milestone this week. It crossed to a distance from Earth of one light-day (about 16 billion miles or 173.14 AU or Earth-sun units) on November 18, 2026. That’s farther than any human-made spacecraft has ever traveled from our home planet.

But objects in space are all moving. And — due to Earth’s own movement — many have noted in past years that Voyager 1’s distance from Earth decreases sometimes. It happens for a few months each year. An astute EarthSky reader asked, does that mean Voyager 1 will get closer to Earth again?

How can they get closer?

It’s true. For a few months each year, Earth in its orbit moves toward the spacecraft faster than the spacecraft are moving away. So the distance between us is decreasing. It can happen because Earth’s motion around the sun is faster than Voyager’s motion. Earth moves through space at a speed of 67,000 miles per hour (30 km/s). Voyager 1 moves at a speed of 38,000 miles per hour (17 km/s). Voyager 2 moves at a speed of 35,000 miles per hour (16 km/s). Incredibly, both Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are slowpokes in contrast to Earth itself!

So Earth can catch up to the Voyagers … sometimes. It only happens for a portion of each year, when Earth comes around a particular side of the sun and is speeding toward the spacecraft faster than they’re moving away. At such times, the distances between Earth and each Voyager are decreasing, not increasing, if only temporarily.

Of course, the Voyagers continue moving at a constant speed, outwards. It’s the relative motion — and therefore distances — between Earth and the spacecraft that changes.

From this video, you can see the trajectory of the Voyager spacecraft as they leave Earth, encounter the outer planets (changing their trajectories), and then head in a straight line outward, out of the solar system.

So what’s the answer?

No, Voyager 1 will never be closer to Earth than 1 light-day again.

By the end of January 2027, Voyager 1 will have gotten as far as 173.58 AU (Earth-sun units) from Earth. At its closest to Earth on April 23, 2027, Voyager 1 will come to 173.31 AU from Earth. But that’s still greater than 1 light-day.

Afterwards, the distance between Earth and Voyager 1 will continue to increase again … until the following northern spring, the spring of 2028, when it’ll be a bit closer to Earth once more — but still farther than a light-day.

Where are Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 now?

Don’t miss the next unmissable night sky event. Sign up to our free newsletter for daily night sky updates, as well as the latest science news.

When will Voyager 2 be 1 light-day away?

Voyager 1’s sister craft, Voyager 2, is on pace to reach one light-day from Earth in November 2035—roughly nine years after Voyager 1 reached the milestone.

That’s true even though Voyager 2 launched 16 days before Voyager 1 in 1977. When it launched, space engineers knew that Voyager 2 would ultimately trail behind Voyager 1. That’s why they named the craft as they did. Voyager 2 it trails behind Voyager 1 for two main reasons:

  • Its route through our solar system was longer: Voyager 2’s route was planned as a slower trajectory through the solar system, so it could visit the outer planets Uranus and Neptune. Its flyby of Neptune’s moon Triton ultimately bent its path southward. It also slightly slowed its outward speed relative to our sun.
  • It travels at a slower speed: As mentioned above, Voyager 1 moves at a speed of 38,000 miles per hour (17 km/s). Voyager 2 moves at a speed of 35,000 miles per hour (16 km/s). So Voyager 1 travels faster. Right now, Voyager 2 sits just over 20 light-hours away from Earth.

When will Voyager 1 be 1 light-day from our sun?

Earth happens to be on the Voyager 1 side of the solar system right now. So, though Voyager 1 achieved a distance of one light-year from Earth on November 18, 2026, it was not one light-year from our sun.

Earth is an average distance of 8 light-minutes from our sun.

Voyager 1 will need several more months to travel those extra light-mintues. Voyager 1 will be 1 light-day from our sun on February 3, 2027.

Read more: Voyager 1 location

Bottom line: The Voyager spacecraft get closer to Earth for a few months every year because Earth moves toward the spacecraft faster in its orbit around the sun than the spacecraft moves away from us. Will Voyager 1 ever get closer than 1 light-day again?

item.title: Mysterious radio signals traced to rare binary star system - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• Astronomers have traced the source of some mysterious radio signals. The signals originate from an unusual pair of stars.
  • The binary system, called GPM J071507-11415, consists of a white dwarf star and sun-like star.
  • The signals come from the white dwarf star and repeat every 8 minutes.

Are you a moon-watcher? Then you’ll love EarthSky’s 2027 lunar calendar, too! Order yours today.

Mysterious radio signals originate from unusual binary star system

Astronomers say they’ve determined the source of a mysterious radio signal that repeats every eight minutes.

No, this regular pulse isn’t coming from some technologically advanced alien race. Scientists at the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) in Australia say the unusual radio signal is originating from a binary pair of stars, where one is a white dwarf and the other is a sunlike star. The white dwarf spins every eight minutes, emitting the radio signals.

And this binary system — GPM J071507-114153 — is rare. Most systems that emit such pulses have red dwarf stars in them. This is the first confirmed case of a regular-radio-signal-producing binary system that contains a white dwarf and a sun-like star.

The researchers published their peer-reviewed results in Nature Astronomy on November 12, 2026.

Long-period transients

Star systems like GPM J071507-114153 are part of a larger grouping called long-period transients (LPTs). These are systems that emit radio pulses that switch on and off over periods ranging from minutes to hours.

Astronomers found the first one in 2021, and about a dozen since then. Several of them contain a white dwarf star. But astronomers didn’t know which star in these binaries was actually emitting the radio signals.

This is the first time that the second star in an LPT binary has been confirmed to be a sun-like star. And the researchers were able to pinpoint the source of the radio signals as close to the white dwarf, or the white dwarf itself. This came after processing more than 100 hours of radio data at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Sam McSweeney at the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) is the lead author of the new study. He said:

This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself.

Mysterious radio signals reveal stellar activity

The radio pulses from the white dwarf enabled the researchers to detect eruptions on the sunlike star, just like those we see on our sun. Co-author Natasha Hurley-Walker at ICRAR said:

As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a ‘stellar prominence,’ which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star’s surface.

It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away.

Telescopic survey yields unusual binary star system

The researchers discovered the GPM J071507-114153 star system as part of a large survey using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA). It scanned the entire Milky Way Galaxy that is visible from Australia.

The researchers are confident that astronomers will find more binary systems like GPM J071507-11415. McSweeney said:

If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built.

Bottom line: Astronomers have discovered that a rare binary star system is the source of mysterious radio signals that repeat every 8 minutes.

item.title: Gegenschein is the elusive glow of interplanetary dust - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Article and most photos via Erwin Matys and Karoline Mrazek of Project Nightflight in Vienna, Austria. Reprinted with permission.

The sun’s counterglow — or gegenschein — is a stargazers’ holy grail. Many amateur astronomers have heard of it, but few have seen it. And fewer still have captured an image of this dim and ghostlike apparition. As a fellow observer put it:

The gegenschein is certainly not a GoTo object.

As a matter of fact, it isn’t an object at all. But let’s start from the beginning.

The 2027 EarthSky lunar calendar makes a great gift. Get yours today!

What is the gegenschein?

The space between the planets isn’t empty. The plane of the solar system is filled with an enormous disk of small dust particles with sizes ranging from less than 1/1000 of a millimeter (0.000039 inches) up to 1 millimeter (0.0394 inches). This interplanetary dust cloud is a highly dynamic structure. In contrast to conventional wisdom, it is not an eons-old leftover from the solar system’s formation. That primordial dust is long gone.

Today’s interplanetary dust is — in an astronomical sense — very young, only millions of years old. Most of the particles originate from quite recent incidents, like asteroid collisions. Some might originate from dust storms on Mars.

Exposed to various forces, the particles do not remain in stationary orbits, but inhabit the disk in ever-changing motion. The smallest particles are swiftly blown out of the solar system by the solar wind. The larger particles don’t survive long either. They tend to collide with larger bodies or slowly spiral into the inner solar system where they fall into the sun.

Nevertheless, asteroid collisions and the erosion of comets constantly replenish the supply of interplanetary dust. So, the interplanetary dust cloud of the solar system is not a static formation, but a dynamic structure consisting of quite young components.

Zodiacal light and gegenschein

For an observer on Earth, this dynamic dust cloud is mainly visible in the form of the zodiacal light. After dusk and before dawn it extends as a cone of light from the sun along the ecliptic path. Often called the false dawn (or false dusk), the zodiacal light is quite bright and can be seen from any observing site that doesn’t suffer from severe light pollution, especially when the ecliptic is high in the sky.

For both hemispheres, springtime is the best time to see the zodiacal light in the evening. And Autumn is the best time to see it before dawn.

The morning and evening zodiacal light are the two areas of the interplanetary dust disk where sunlight gets forward scattered to Earth, resulting in the bright silvery light cones. The interplanetary dust disk is also visible along the rest of the ecliptic path, where it is known as the zodiacal band.

And at the point directly opposite the sun, the geometry again works in our favor and enhances the visibility of the interplanetary dust. This is the area of the gegenschein.

Brighter when opposite the sun

But why does the gegenschein glow brighter than the rest of the zodiacal band? Looking at the interplanetary dust disk from Earth, the section at the antisolar point is illuminated from directly behind our heads. This results in an increase in brightness called the opposition effect.

The opposition effect is a frequent phenomenon for solar system bodies. For example, the moon shows a significant peak in brightness around full moon, i.e. at its opposition. Another example is Saturn’s rings in the days around opposition, when they brighten drastically.

You may have also seen this effect when on an airplane. Read more: How can you see an airplane glory?

The gegenschein effect on Earth

The main reason for this brightening during opposition is shadow hiding, meaning that all particles are fully illuminated. You can see this opposition effect here on Earth during daylight if you’re outdoors and look at the ground in front of you. If the ground is sufficiently coarse, you’ll see a brightening around the shadow of your head. To document this phenomenon, we made the photo below, which shows the effect on volcanic gravel.

Interestingly, the brightening around the camera’s shadow had an apparent diameter of 10 degrees, about the same size as the diameter of the gegenschein in the night sky. Next time you walk on a rough surface in sunlight, look for this terrestrial version of the counterglow.

To sum up, the gegenschein is not an object. It’s a play of light on the solar system’s interplanetary dust disk. The section of the dust at the antisolar point is squarely illuminated, resulting in a brightness enhancement due to shadow hiding. This so-called opposition effect can be encountered at many occasions, but with the gegenschein it makes its most ghostlike and outlandish appearance. This is probably the reason why it is such a prized trophy among amateur astronomers.

Gegenschein under dark skies

From our observing and photography sessions at dark-sky sites, the gegenschein was a familiar companion. Out under the stars, sooner or later one of us would mention:

Hmm, the gegenschein is quite obvious tonight …

… followed by the typical reply:

Yep, bright and shiny!

This short dialogue would indicate that our eyes had reached full dark adaptation and our night vision was at maximum capacity. We often talked about making an image of our good old dark-sky companion, the gegenschein. But for some reason it never happened. Other projects were in the way, on other occasions the position in the sky was not right or the atmosphere’s transparency was just not good enough.

How we captured the gegenschein

But on the night from October 30 to 31, 2019, we finally did give it a go. On October 30 we were already several days on an imaging excursion on La Palma island. During daytime the annoying Calima weather pattern had finally stopped and skies were again as deep blue and transparent as they can be on this beautiful island. Accommodated in a solitary finca far away from inhabited areas and about 800 meters (2,600 feet) above sea level, we had the perfect conditions for photographing the gegenschein.

Around midnight, when the counterglow culminates, our instruments registered a sky brightness of 21.4 magnitudes per square arcsecond in the zenith. This is so dark that Sirius noticeably brightened the landscape when it rose behind a mountain ridge later that night.

The gegenschein itself was pretty obvious to the unaided eye. Below the constellation Aries the Ram, directly on the ecliptic path, a distinct glow about 10 degrees across marked the antisolar point. The very faint zodiacal band crossing the whole sky was visible too, almost looking like an artificial marking of the ecliptic. Under these conditions, shooting the gegenschein was an easy task.

Details, details

For those interested in the technical details: We made 23 unfiltered exposures of 4 minutes with a 16mm lens @f/5.6 on a Baader-modified 1100D Canon DSLR. For sky tracking we used a purely mechanical device, the Mini Track LX2. This innovative device is a frequent companion on our imaging excursions. For those interested in more details, we provide a thorough review of the Mini Track LX2 for download on our website.

The total weight of our imaging gear was less than 3 kilograms (6.6 pounds), including camera and tripod. The 23 individual exposures of the gegenschein were later calibrated, registered and stacked with DeepSkyStacker. Processing of the final image was done in Photoshop, where we applied substantial contrast enhancement.

How you can see the gegenschein

If you’ve never encountered the gegenschein yourself, don’t expect it to be as prominent as in the photograph at the top of this post. We applied heavy contrast enhancement to the image to make the counterglow, its shape and its size better visible. To our human eyes, even under the best conditions, the gegenschein is an elusive and dim glow.

On several occasions we compared the visual brightness of the counterglow and sections of the Milky Way. We always found it to be about as bright as the dimmest parts of the winter Milky Way. The stretch of the Milky Way that approximates the counterglow’s brightness best is the section between the star Mirfak and the asterism called the Kids, next to Capella. That’s very dim. Any bright object in its vicinity (e.g. Jupiter or Mars at opposition) makes it hard to observe.

Aside from being slightly brighter in the middle and fading out uniformly in all directions, the gegenschein shows no structure at all. It has a roundish form, circular or elliptical, measuring approximately 10 degrees across. That is about the size of a fist stretched out at arm’s length.

Follow these 5 tips to see the gegenschein for yourself.

Tip 1: Check the position

Before you begin searching for the gegenschein in the night sky, you should check its current position. The map below helps you know where to look. It also shows you whether the counterglow is detectable at all, because its visibility highly depends on its position against the starry background.

In June, July and December it is completely invisible, because it is in front of the Milky Way. Other obstacles can be the bright planets Mars and Jupiter. When one of them is near opposition, it is in the same region of the sky as the counterglow and may outshine it.

Some planetarium programs or stargazing apps might also be useful tools to determine the position of the gegenschein. If the software provides an option to display the center of Earth’s shadow, this will show you the current antisolar point.

Tip 2: Look for it at maximum height above the horizon

The gegenschein is always highest above the horizon around local midnight, so that’s the best time of the night to give an observation a try. There should also be no moon above the horizon. But that’s not all. Like the sun itself, the antisolar point too has different culmination heights during the course of the year.

For observers in the Northern Hemisphere, the antisolar point has its highest culmination at the winter solstice around December 21. Sadly, during December the gegenschein is in front of the winter Milky Way and therefore invisible. So, the best months to see the gegenschein from northern latitudes are November and January.

For Southern Hemisphere observers, the largest culmination height of the antisolar point happens at summer solstice around June 21. For southerners too, the Milky Way is in the way. Again, one should look before or after the solstice, in this case during May or August.

Tip 3: Try from the best observing location you have access to

You can’t see the gegenschein from light-polluted sites. Even moderate light pollution diminishes the counterglow’s contrast too much. Based on our observations, the absolute minimum to detect the gegenschein is a sky brightness of 21.0 mag/arcsecond2 in the zenith. But this applies only if you are already quite familiar with the gegenschein and know exactly where to look.

For first-time observers, we recommend a site with a sky brightness of 21.2 mag/arcsecond2 in the zenith or better. These conditions only exist far from cities or other inhabited areas. Observing sites in the mountains especially qualify because of the reduced air mass at higher altitudes above sea level.

Tip 4: Wait for favorable weather conditions

Even if you observe from a dark-sky location, the average clear sky might not be good enough for seeing the gegenschein. What you really want is a night sky with exceptionally high transparency. This will only be the case if the air mass above your observing site is as dry as possible.

To get an idea of the current situation at your location, you can use a website that provides weather forecasts for astronomical observations. Sites like this display data about humidity at all tropospheric layers. Another condition for high transparency would be that the air is clean, i.e. free of dust. At mid-latitudes, the necessary conditions of dry and clean air often occur after the passage of a cold front or a trough.

Tip 5: Expand your observing skills

Given you have good eyesight in the dark and that you already have some observing experience, there are several observing techniques you need to master.

First, you need to learn how to become truly dark adapted. This might put your patience to a test, since your eyes need at least 3/4 of an hour to fully adjust to the dark. So, no smartphones or other handheld devices during this time. You should only use very dim red lights if you don’t want to ruin your night vision.

A second technique you might need for seeing the gegenschein is averted vision. With averted vision, you do not look directly at an object but a little off to the side while continuing to concentrate on the object. This way you are using peripheral vision, which is more sensitive to low light levels than the center of the eye. Some observers report that this technique makes a big difference for them, and it might help you too. In any case, hunting down the gegenschein will improve your observing skills a lot. Besides, it makes a highly interesting project and sooner or later you, too, will be able to put that prized stargazer’s trophy on your shelf.

What is Project Nightflight?

About Project Nightflight: “Our mission is the starry sky. We internationally promote the conservation of the starry sky as environmental resource. item.description:
To be read in conjunction with the Tangent section of the astrophiz podcast #245

https://astrophiz.com/2026/10/29/astrophiz-245-november-sky-guide-a-daylight-occultation-of-jupiter-mars-and-jupiter-close-together-uranus-at-opposition-and-the-leonid-storms-to-come/

 

Morning sky looking north-east as seen from Adelaide at 4:00 am AEDST on Wednesday 18 November  showing Leo, with the Leonid Meteor shower radiant indicated with a starburst. 


Similar views will be seen elsewhere at the equivalent local time . Click to embiggen.

 The starburst indicates the radiant, the apparent point of origin of the meteors (they can actually first appear much further away from the radiant).

 

Today is the 60th anniversary of the Spectacular Leonid storm of 1966 (and the 25th anniversary of the 2001 storm). The Leonids are an iconic meteor shower due to spectacular displays roughly every 33 years, with major storms in 1833, 1966, 2001 and 2002. 

I particularly remember the 2001 Leonids, which I saw from Alice Springs. Meteors streaming above my head like rain. 

Since then the Leonids have not been spectacular, this year under good conditions we can only expect to see around 3 per hour from Australia (from a ZHR of 15, The figure ZHR is zenithal hourly rate. This is the number of meteors that a single observer would see per hour if the shower's "point of origin", or radiant, were at the zenith and the sky was dark enough for 6.5-magnitude stars to be visible to the naked eye. In Australia the radiant does not get near the Zenith). 

Meteor showers are predicable; they are the dust trails of comets (and the Asteroid Phaeton). Following the orbit of the parent comet and occurring at yearly intervals almost like clockwork as we cross the dust streams of emitted by the parent object. 

Comet storms are not so predictable (or weren’t until seminal work back in 1999-2000 on the Leonid storms). The Leonids are due to dusty debris from Comet Tempel-Tuttle slamming into Earth's atmosphere. The next perihelion of the Leonids’ parent comet, 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is due on May 20, 2031, so we should expect elevated rates around then. 

Now, while Leonid meteor storms roughly coincide with the perihelion passage of the comet, the storms themselves are NOT due to the dust generated during perihelion passage, but older dust streams, the 2001 Leonids were due to impacts from the dust streams emitted centuries earlier in 1667, 1866 and 1699. 

How can we decide that these dust streams are responsible? We model the behavior of dust emitted that those times, we know the orbit and the gravitation and non-gravitational (such as radiation pressure) on the dust trails, along with the resonance effects of Jupiter and an estimate of the ejection velocity of the dust grains. 

From these we can model the obits of the ejected dust plumes and see when they will cross earths path, The predictions were spectacularly successful for 1999 and 2001, with accurate predictions of timing an a bit of an overestimate on the rates (but still predicting storms). Reviews of two decades of predictions  conclude that peak times are routinely predicted to ±0.5 h. Rates not so much. 

A new model has predicted storm conditions for 2033 to 2034. This model improves the analysis of dust ejection sites, fitted to comet observations. Error minimization was achieved by looking at past predictions and actual results, with more detailed modelling of the dust particles.

Date and timeRateLocation
2033: November 17th, 22:56 UTZHR=~1400 meteors per hour.Timing favours Asia.
2034: two peaks. 1st peak: November 18th, 3:30 UTC,ZHR=~1400 meteors per hour.Timing favours Europe, Africa.
2034:2nd peak: November 18th, 23:45 UTZHR=~1200 meteors per hour. Peak favours: Asia, Europe, Africa. Europe & Africa get a meteor storm two nights in a row!
2035: no storm, still a strong outburst. November 19th, 14:16 UTZHR=~650 meteors per hour.Timing favours the Far East.

Often there are increases in the Leonid rates 3-4 years before the comet Temple-Tuttle's perihelion, but new  model (and some older models) suggest that there will be pretty much background rates until 2033.

item.title: Leonid meteor shower: All you need to know in 2026 - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
Mid-November meteors … the Leonids

Predicted peak: The peak is predicted** for 0 UTC on November 18, 2026.
When to watch: The midnight to dawn hours — on the mornings of November 17 and November 18 — are likely best. And this year, near the radiant point of the Leonids meteor shower, you’ll spot Jupiter and Mars, separated by only about two full-moon widths.
Radiant: Rises around midnight, highest in the sky at dawn. You’ll see more meteors after the radiant has come over the eastern horizon. Do you need to look at the radiant to see the meteors? No. The meteors will fly from that single point in the sky, but they’ll appear all over the sky.
Nearest moon phase: In 2026, the 1st quarter moon falls at 11:48 UTC on November 17. A 1st quarter moon sets around midnight. So the moon won’t interfere with the Leonids in 2026.
Expected meteors at peak, under ideal conditions: Under a dark sky with no moon, you might see 10 to 15 Leonid meteors per hour.

The 2027 lunar calendar from EarthSky is now available! See the moon’s phase for every day of the year. Get yours now!

A meteor storm in 2026?

Earth is passing through the Leonid meteor stream in space from October 28 through December 7. You might see a Leonid meteor at any time during that period, especially if you’re out under a dark sky.

The Leonid meteor shower is famous! But why, when the hourly rate is so low, just 10-15 meteors per hour? The Leonids’ fame stems from its periodic meteor storms. The Leonids produced the first major meteor storm of modern times on November 12-13, 1833. It’s often called The Night the Stars Fell. We can’t know the meteor rate exactly. But a widely accepted estimate suggests a rate of up to 2,500 meteors per minute (approximately 150,000 meteors per hour), with some observers reporting seeing up to 20 to 70 meteors per second at the storm’s absolute climax.

Leonids also produced one of the greatest storms in living memory — with rates as high as in the 1833 storm for a period of about 15-20 minutes — on the morning of November 17, 1966. Some who witnessed it reported having a strong impression of Earth moving through space, as our world forded the meteor stream. “I almost felt as if I needed to grip the ground,” one observer told EarthSky.

Leonid meteor storms sometimes recur in cycles of 33 to 34 years. But the Leonids around the turn of the century — while wonderful for many observers — did not match the shower of 1966.

Alas! In most years, the Lion whimpers rather than roars. And scientists don’t expect a Leonid meteor storm this year.

Still, the shower should be fun to watch! Find a dark place to watch at EarthSky’s Best Places to Stargaze page.

Report a fireball (very bright meteor) to the American Meteor Society: it’s fun and easy

Read more: Veteran meteor photographer Eliot Herman’s website: Meteor Photography

The parent comet of the Leonid meteor shower

From the late, great Don Machholz (1952-2022), who discovered 12 comets …

Periodic Comet Tempel-Tuttle, officially known as 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is responsible for the Leonid meteor shower. Wilhelm Tempel of Marseille Observatory in France discovered this comet on the evening of December 19, 1865. He found the comet in the northern sky, located in a part of the sky under the North Star near the star Beta Ursae Minoris.

Word of the comet discovery became known throughout Europe. But the news had not yet spread to the United States. Horace Tuttle of Harvard College Observatory picked up the comet 17 days later, on the evening of January 5, 1866. Because this was an independent discovery, Tuttle’s name was added to the comet. Based upon the measurements during this visit of the comet, scientists calculated an orbit of 33.17 years. Astronomers quickly realized that the meteor storm of 1833 — and the annual meteor showers that occurred in mid-November of each year — were the result of this comet.

One would think there’d have been interest in recovering this comet as it came back to Earth’s vicinity in 1899. But there wasn’t much interest in seeing the comet that year. Everyone wanted to see a meteor storm. So, observers missed the comet in 1899. Also missing was a great meteor storm that year.

Scientists expected the next return in 1932. The observatories, using photographic plates with narrow field-of-view telescopes, missed it then too. And again, a major meteor shower did not materialize.

The comet was finally recovered in 1965. The brightest the comet got that year was 16th magnitude, visible only in very large telescopes. But the spectacular meteor storm of 1966 followed!

On the next return, in early 1998, the comet was bright enough that you could see it in binoculars. This pass produced additional impressive meteor showers, which stretched across several years in 1999-2001. 

55P/Tempel-Tuttle is due back in early 2031.

Leonid meteor storms in recent history

Most astronomers say you need more than 1,000 meteors an hour to consider a shower a storm. That’s far from the 10 to 15 meteors per hour the Leonids deliver in average years.

The Leonid’s parent comet, Tempel-Tuttle, completes a single orbit around the sun about once every 33 years. It releases fresh material every time it approaches the sun. Since the 19th century, skywatchers have looked for Leonid meteor storms about every 33 years, beginning with the meteor storm of 1833, which witnesses said produced up to 150,000 meteors per hour.

The next great Leonid storms were about 33 years later, in 1866 and 1867. In 1899, a meteor storm did not materialize. In fact, the anticipation of a great meteor storm was so high — and the results so disappointing — that many astronomers felt it was the worst blow ever suffered by astronomy in the eyes of the public.

Not until 1966 did the next spectacular Leonid storm happen, this time over the Americas. In 1966, observers in the southwest United States reported seeing up to 70 meteors per second during a span of 15-20 minutes on the morning of November 17, 1966.

Then came the 1999-2001 showers.

  • 1999: Observed rates peaked on November 18 at approximately 3,700 to 4,000 meteors per hour. The peak lasted for a short window and was best seen from Europe, North Africa and the Middle East.
  • 2000: Rates dropped considerably in contrast to 1999, but Earth still encountered multiple dust trails. Rates peaked at approximately 130 to 480 meteors per hour, hampered somewhat by bright moonlight.
  • 2001: The Leonids returned with a major double peak on November 18–19.
    • First Peak: Produced 1,500 to 2,000 meteors per hour, best seen from North America and Hawaii.
    • Second Peak: Reached 3,000 to 3,700 meteors per hour, matching or slightly exceeding the peak intensity of the 1999 storm. Best seen from East Asia and Australia.

item.title: Mars Sample Return: NASA’s new effort to bring samples home - Tonight | EarthSky
item.description:
• Mars Sample Return was NASA’s original plan to bring samples of Martian rocks and sand back to Earth. Scientists would then study them in laboratories, looking for clues about the planet’s wet past and possible signs of microbial life.
  • NASA has now proposed a new strategy to bring those samples home. Will it work?
  • Previous proposals were considered too expensive, and the estimated time needed to return the samples to Earth was too long.

Are you a moon-watcher? Then you’ll love EarthSky’s 2027 lunar calendar! Order yours today.

Mars Sample Return still alive?

The Mars Sample Return concept was scrapped — and declared dead — due to ballooning costs and a too-long timeframe. But the Mars Perseverance rover has already collected samples. It’s possible they contain evidence of ancient microbial life on Mars. So scientists are itching to have the samples returned to Earth. And now NASA has announced a new plan.

Tiffany Morgan, director of the Mars Exploration Program, detailed NASA’s new Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture on November 9, 2026, during a virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group. The new retrieval architecture provides a framework that NASA could build the actual mission upon. The idea now is to develop “impartial recommendations” for the mission. For example, the architecture will cover proposed mission requirements, review previous lessons learned and evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options.

There will also be a Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture strategy team kickoff in January 2027. A final report will be due in winter 2027-2028.

Leonard David wrote about the new concept for Space.com and Leonard David’s INSIDE OUTER SPACE on November 10, 2026.

A new strategy for Mars Sample Return

The framework of the new strategy is as follows:

  • Develop impartial recommendations for retrieving the Martian samples collected by NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover and deliver them to Earth
  • Assess proposed mission requirements
  • Review prior lessons learned
  • Evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options

A previous proposal would have cost an estimated $11 billion by 2024. And the samples wouldn’t have been returned to Earth until 2040. NASA determined that was too long and too expensive.

Another effort would cost $8 billion, with a return to Earth by 2035.

Perseverance rover’s priceless samples

The Perseverance rover has obtained numerous samples from Martian rocks. They are stored in small tubes. Some tubes are kept within the rover for analysis and others are left on the ground, waiting — hopefully — to be picked up later in a sample return mission. The rover had collected 33 samples by 2025.

Meanwhile, Perseverance is still exploring a region just outside the rim of Jezero crater. It still has a few sample tubes left, but not too many.

Read more: NASA’s Perseverance rover on Mars sets off-world driving record

Signs of ancient life?

One of the most important — and exciting — samples comes from a rock called Cheyava Falls. It lies in an ancient riverbed that dried up billions of years ago.

Perseverance found odd rings and dots on the rock that looked like leopard spots and poppy seeds. They highly resembled formations on rocks on Earth created by microbes. Could they be signs of ancient life?

The rover itself can’t determine for sure their origins, however. The samples need to be studied in more advanced labs on Earth. This is the primary reason these samples are so important. They could hold evidence of ancient microbial life. And we can’t bring them home yet.

Risks for future human missions

There is another element to the sample return quest as well. It involves the risks to future human astronauts landing on Mars. There could be compounds in the samples or other rocks or sand that are toxic and dangerous to humans.

Bruce Jakosky of the University of Colorado Boulder and the University of Washington told Space.com:

The purpose is to understand the risk to astronauts and to hardware. The risk includes that from compounds that are present in the soil that are hazardous to astronauts if breathed in. This includes perchlorates and chloromethanes that have been identified already, and detection of other species that might be present. It also includes dust that can be breathed in by astronauts and that can affect hardware wear and tear.

Mars Sample Return 1st, then astronauts

Jakosky explained why it’s important to bring the samples back to Earth before human missions to Mars. This includes astronaut safety as a top priority:

  • Identify and characterize known hazardous chemicals to ensure astronaut safety (e.g., perchlorates and chloromethanes), and look for possible additional hazardous chemicals
  • Characterize very fine dust particles that could cause respiratory issues in astronauts
  • Characterize dust and regolith properties for spacesuit design and wear patterns
  • Search in advance of the arrival of humans for evidence of extant life that could interact with terrestrial life
  • Enhance astronaut effectiveness on the surface and science return from human missions by providing initial context and analysis
  • Demonstrate successful round-trip to Mars
  • Demonstrate successful round-trip travel, including entry, descent, landing and ascent from the surface of Mars.
  • Demonstrate implementation of planetary protection protocols. While human missions would not use the same approaches, what we learn from doing these would make the approach for humans much easier to plan and implement.

China’s sample return mission

Meanwhile, China is pushing ahead with its own sample return mission. The complex Tianwen-3 mission will have a lander, an ascender, a service capsule, an orbiter and an Earth reentry module.

China is looking to launch the mission by 2028 and bring the samples back to Earth by 2031.

Bottom line: NASA has begun a new effort for a Mars Sample Return mission to bring the highly-sought samples from the Perseverance rover back to Earth.

Mountain-sized asteroid to pass close to Earth on August 7, 2027

A space rock around 800 to 1,800 meters wide (about 0.5 to 1.1 miles) is set to soar close by Earth on August 7, 2027.

The asteroid — named 1999 AN10 — has been labelled potentially hazardous by NASA, but there is no chance of it impacting Earth in 2027. It will safely pass us in August with a separation of about 389,855 kilometers (242,240 miles), or roughly the same distance away as the moon.

If the asteroid is not going to hit us, why is it labeled a potentially hazardous asteroid? A potentially hazardous asteroid is any space rock that comes as close as 0.05 astronomical units (AU) from Earth and that’s larger than 140 meters (460 feet) in diameter. The label reflects the potential that at some point in the future — if this large space rock gets nudged by another passing object — its orbit could be altered in a way that would cause it to hit Earth. Currently, 1999 AN10 has a zero chance of hitting Earth during its 2027 flyby.

So this isn’t something to be scared of. But it is something to get excited about! The asteroid is so big and will come so close that you’ll be able to spot it with binoculars as it glides by. 1999 AN10 will peak around magnitude 7.3 as it passes through the night sky over North and South America. Its closest approach is at 7:12:05 UTC on August 7, 2027. That would be 2:12:05 am CDT on August 7 for the Americas.

Overnight on August 7, 2027, asteroid 1999 AN10 will pass through the constellations Taurus, Aries, Pisces and Pegasus.

Will asteroid 1999 AN10 hit the moon?

If the asteroid will pass about 1 lunar distance from Earth, does that mean it could hit the moon? How close will it get to the moon?

Well, moon lovers, don’t worry. The closest the asteroid will come to the moon is 763,391 km, or 474,349 miles. That’s about twice as far as it will get from Earth! So, as you might have guessed, it means the asteroid will pass Earth on the opposite side to the moon at that time.

More about potentially hazardous asteroids

Astronomers discovered 1999 AN10 on January 13, 1999, at the Lincoln Laboratory Experimental Test Site in New Mexico. It’s an Apollo-class asteroid, meaning its orbit crosses Earth’s orbit around the sun.

The asteroid travels around the sun once every 643 days, following an elongated orbit that takes it from inside Earth’s orbit to well beyond Mars’ orbit.

It’s a potentially hazardous asteroid because of its large size. NASA says any impactor larger than 1 to 2 kilometers (.6 to 1.2 miles) in size would have worldwide effects. It could blast massive amounts of dust into the atmosphere, dimming sunlight for months and threatening global civilization.

Astronomers have cataloged roughly 2,500 known potentially hazardous asteroids. But they estimate that’s only about half of the population. However, they believe they have found 90% of the biggest potentially hazardous asteroids.

Other notable potentially hazardous asteroids

99942 Apophis

  • Close approach: April 13, 2029
  • Distance: About 32,000 km (20,000 miles) above Earth’s surface
  • Size: Approximately 375 meters (1,230 feet)

Apophis will pass closer to Earth than many geostationary satellites. Scientists once worried about a possible future collision, but additional observations ruled out an impact risk for at least 100 years. NASA’s OSIRIS-APEX spacecraft will study it after the encounter.

101955 Bennu

  • Potential impact date: September 24, 2182
  • Size: About 500 meters (1/3 mile) wide
  • Impact odds: Approximately 1 in 2,700 for that date, according to NASA’s 2021 orbital analysis.

NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission collected a sample from Bennu and returned it to Earth in 2023. Scientists are studying the sample to learn about the early solar system.

2001 WN5

  • Close approach: June 26, 2028
  • Distance: About 248,700 km (154,500 miles) from Earth’s center
  • Size: Approximately 940 meters (0.58 mile)

This asteroid will pass inside the moon’s orbit. It will be a bit brighter than 1999 AN10, peaking at magnitude 6.7.

1997 XF11

  • Closest approach: October 26, 2028
  • Distance: About 929,000 km (577,000 miles) from Earth
  • Size: Approximately 700 meters (0.43 mile)

This asteroid attracted considerable attention after its discovery in 1997. Early calculations suggested a possible future collision. Better observations ruled that out.

Read more:
Apophis: From scary asteroid to a rare science opportunity
11,000 new asteroids! Astronomers call it ‘tip of iceberg’
This active asteroid has grown a tail! What happened?

Bottom line: Asteroid 1999 AN10, which might be a mile wide, will pass Earth on August 7, 2027, about 1 lunar distance away. The encounter poses no danger.

The 2027 EarthSky Lunar Calendar is now available! A unique and beautiful poster-sized calendar. Keep up with all phases of the moon every night of the year. Order yours today!

Mirach, also known as Beta Andromedae, is a star in the constellation Andromeda. It’s only moderately bright. But it’s an important star to stargazers, as it can act as a signpost to three galaxies: the Andromeda galaxy (M31), the Triangulum galaxy (M33) and a galaxy known as Mirach’s Ghost (NGC 404).

Mirach is what’s known as a red giant star, a star in the final stages of its evolution whose outer layers have expanded. It has about three to four times the sun’s mass and 100 times the sun’s diameter. It shines with about 1,900 times our sun’s total brightness. But Mirach is rather far away, at 200 light-years. That’s why it shines in our sky at only 2nd magnitude, a respectable brightness but not as bright as many other stars.

But it’s bright enough to be a useful signpost to three galaxies. Read on to find out how to spot them.

Finding the Andromeda galaxy with Mirach

Draw an imaginary line from Mirach to the star Mu (µ) Andromedae (see below). Then, continue extending that line for about the same distance between those two stars to reach the Andromeda Galaxy.

Under dark, moonless skies, the Andromeda galaxy appears as a smudge in the sky to the unaided eye. Even if the moon is out or under skies with moderate light pollution (like the suburbs), you can see it through binoculars. At about 2.5 million light-years away, the Andromeda galaxy is the nearest large spiral galaxy to our Milky Way. And it’s the most distant thing you can easily see with your eye alone.

Finding the Triangulum galaxy (M33)

The Triangulum Galaxy (M33), in the constellation Triangulum, is much fainter than the Andromeda Galaxy. Some people with excellent eyesight have been able to see it unaided by telescopes or binoculars, in extraordinarily good viewing conditions. Even so, it can still be a challenge to find M33 with binoculars and small telescopes.

To find Triangulum, you’ll use the same two stars as above, but star-hop in the opposite direction. Follow an imaginary line from the star Mu (µ) Andromedae to Mirach, then continue to draw that line past Mirach, for twice the distance between Mu Andromedae and Mirach, to reach the Triangulum Galaxy.

Finding Mirach’s Ghost (NGC 404)

When you look at Mirach, you’re looking almost exactly in the direction of the galaxy labeled NGC 404 but known affectionately among astronomers as Mirach’s Ghost. That’s because the remote, fuzzy galaxy lies right next to the moderately bright star, just 1/10 degree from Mirach. A full moon is 1/2 degree wide, so you can see that’s very close.

Mirach’s Ghost is faint, just magnitude 11 in brightness. Many amateur astronomers try to spot it with their small telescopes, but due to its proximity to the brighter 2nd-magnitude Mirach, seeing the galaxy is not easy.

NGC 404 is located about 10 million light-years away, just beyond our Local Group of galaxies. The Local Group is a cluster of galaxies that includes the Milky Way, Andromeda and Triangulum galaxies. NGC 404 does not appear gravitationally bound to our Local Group.

Bottom line: Stargazers use Mirach, a moderately bright star in the constellation Andromeda, to locate three galaxies. It can help you find the Andromeda Galaxy, the Triangulum Galaxy and a galaxy known as Mirach’s Ghost (NGC 404).
